page.title: Virtual Event Timeline Planning Guide
page.description: A step‑by‑step timeline for webinars, summits and hybrid conferences, covering phases, owners, tools, rehearsals and delivery.
page.h1: How long does a virtual event take?
page.definition: A virtual event timeline is a structured schedule that maps every production phase from intake through publishing, assigns an owner to each workstream, and sets concrete dates for rehearsals, live delivery and post‑event assets. It also defines backup paths, approval gates and the hand‑off to marketing for follow‑up.
page.quick_answer: Start a webinar three to four weeks out and a summit six to eight weeks out; lock platform and venue AV early, then run a full rehearsal two to five days before go‑live.

sections.h2: What are the main phases of a virtual event timeline?

blocks.p: The timeline follows seven sequential phases, each with a single owner and a tangible output.

ul: Intake – gather goals, audience size and budget
Brief – write run of show, speaker briefs and slide template
Production – build graphics, configure platform and test encoder
Review – internal QA of assets and run‑through with speakers
Approval – sign‑off from stakeholder and compliance
Publishing – go live, record and push to on‑demand library
Reporting – compile attendance, engagement and survey data

blocks.p: Dependencies flow forward; a delay in brief pushes production, review and approval later, so each phase must close before the next begins.

sections.h2: How far in advance should I plan a webinar versus a summit?

blocks.p: A webinar needs three to four weeks of lead time while a summit or hybrid conference requires six to eight weeks.

ol: Lock platform and, for hybrid, venue AV contracts
Confirm speakers and collect presentation files
Create run of show and branded lower‑third templates
Schedule full rehearsal two to five days before live date
Execute technical check sixty minutes before start
Deliver edited recording and clips within one to two days

blocks.p: For hybrid events the venue AV agreement must be signed before the agenda is final, because room layout dictates camera positions and ingest points.

sections.h2: Which workstreams need owners and what do they deliver?

blocks.p: Eight workstreams each have a named owner and a concrete deliverable that feeds the next stage.

head: Workstream
Owner
Output
rows: Configured event space, backup stream URL
Run of show, branded graphics, lower thirds
Attendance dashboard, engagement metrics, survey results

blocks.p: West Peek Productions can staff any of these roles on the platform you already use, ensuring a single point of accountability for the live show.

sections.h2: What tools are commonly used for scheduling, briefs, publishing and reporting?

blocks.p: Teams typically adopt a small stack that covers planning, collaboration, distribution and measurement.

ul: Project plan – Asana, Monday.com or Airtable
Briefs and scripts – Google Docs or Notion
Analytics – GA4 and HubSpot or Salesforce

blocks.p: Integrating the project plan with the publishing CMS via Zapier or Make automates hand‑offs and reduces manual copy‑paste errors.

sections.h2: When should rehearsals, technical checks and replay delivery happen?

blocks.p: Rehearsal and check timing protect the live experience and the post‑event assets.

ul: Full rehearsal on the real platform two to five days before go‑live
Technical check sixty minutes before start, including backup stream verification
Edited replay and highlight clips delivered within one to two days after the event

blocks.p: A post‑event debrief within the same week captures lessons learned and feeds the next planning cycle.

faq.q: What is the minimum lead time for a simple webinar?
faq.a: A simple webinar can be ready in three to four weeks if the platform is already chosen, speakers are confirmed and a single producer handles the run of show. This timeline includes brief creation, slide template design, a full rehearsal and a backup stream test.

faq.q: How many people are needed to run a hybrid summit?
faq.a: A hybrid summit typically requires a show caller, a speaker manager, a moderator, a platform operator and a producer, so at least five dedicated roles share the workload. Each role owns a workstream such as venue AV, remote ingest, audience chat and post‑event reporting.

faq.q: When should the final recording be sent to attendees?
faq.a: Deliver the edited recording and highlight clips within one to two days after the live session while the content is still fresh in participants’ minds. Include a short thank‑you note, a link to the on‑demand library and a quick survey for feedback.

faq.q: What backup plan should be in place for streaming failures?
faq.a: Run a parallel backup stream on a second encoder or a secondary platform, assign a producer to monitor both feeds and switch instantly if the primary drops. Document the switch procedure in the run of show and rehearse it during the technical check.

faq.q: Can the same timeline be reused for recurring webinars?
faq.a: Yes, a repeat format can move faster because the run of show, slide template and speaker brief are already approved; only dates and promotion need updating. Plan two to three weeks from brief to live for each new episode, keeping the same rehearsal and backup steps.
